teaser: The most famous kiss in sculpture was meant for the gates of Hell.
review_notes:
Catalog year 1889; the marble was commissioned by the French state in 1888 and carved between about 1888 and 1898, after a model of about 1882.
Height about 181.5 cm.
Carving of the marble by the practitioner Jean Turcan: per Musée Rodin, please verify.
Rodin's remark calling the group a large knick-knack ('un grand bibelot') made to the usual formula: widely quoted, wording varies.
The English marble (now Tate) hidden under a sheet at Lewes Town Hall around 1914: standard account, please verify the details.
This photo shows the group from the side where the faces are hidden and the book in Paolo's left hand is not visible. A museum visitor sits behind at left and a bronze bust stands at right.

lesson.text: Can you make people feel a kiss without showing them a single face? From where this photograph was taken, in the Musée Rodin in Paris, that is the test. Her raised arm and his bent head close over the meeting of the lips like a door. You have to read everything else.

lesson.title: A kiss told by limbs
lesson.text: Three places where the bodies speak for the hidden faces.

spots.title: Her arm
spots.text: It hooks around his neck and pulls his head down. In 1880s sculpture women were usually kissed. Here she is the one who draws him in.

spots.title: His hand
spots.text: A large hand with spread fingers rests on her hip. It sits there lightly, as if he does not yet dare to hold on.

spots.title: Her leg over his
spots.text: She has swung her thigh across his knee. Her whole body leans into him, while his back stays almost upright.

lesson.text: So the eagerness is hers and the hesitation is his. That balance comes from a story. The pair are Paolo and Francesca, two real people of 13th-century Italy whom the poet Dante placed in his “Inferno”. She was married to his brother. The husband caught them and killed them both.

In Dante's poem, the two fall in love while reading aloud the tale of Lancelot and Guinevere. Rodin put the book in Paolo's other hand, slipping from his fingers. It is on the far side of the group and cannot be seen from this angle.

Auguste Rodin first modeled the couple around 1882 as a small group for “The Gates of Hell”, a giant bronze doorway covered with the damned. Then he took them off. They looked too happy among so much suffering. Shown alone a few years later, the lovers lost their names, and critics simply called the piece “The Kiss”.
In 1888 the French state ordered a version in marble, bigger than life: the block stands about 1.8 m high (6 ft). It took ten years. When it finally went on show in 1898, the public adored it.

Rodin did not carve it. Like most sculptors of his day, he modeled in clay and handed the stone to skilled assistants. A carver named Jean Turcan cut most of this marble, enlarging Rodin's model point by point.
One choice in the stone is pure Rodin, though, and this photo shows it well. The marble has two completely different surfaces, and each one makes the other stronger.

spots.title: The rock seat
spots.text: Under the lovers the block is left rough, pitted with tool marks. It looks like stone that was simply quarried and never worked.

spots.title: His back and arm
spots.text: Here the marble is rubbed to a soft glow. Light from the window slides over shoulder and ribs, and the stone starts to read as skin.

spots.title: Her feet
spots.text: One foot is planted with the toes pressed down, the other tucks in behind it. The smooth ankles grow straight out of the coarse rock.

spots.title: His foot
spots.text: His toes grip the edge of the base far out on the left. His legs are spread wide to make room for her.

spots.title: The base
spots.text: A wide skirt of chiseled stone carries the whole group. You can follow the short, parallel strokes of the carver's tools.

spots.title: A measure of scale
spots.text: The visitor seated by the window gives you the size. The lovers, even sitting down, tower over him.

lesson.text: Rodin borrowed that contrast from Michelangelo, whose unfinished figures seem to struggle out of raw stone. Next to the rough block, the polished bodies look warmer and softer than marble has any right to be. It also reminds you that all this tenderness is one rock.

A second marble was ordered by a collector living in the English town of Lewes. Lent to the town hall around 1914, it was soon surrounded by a railing and covered with a sheet, for fear it would excite the soldiers billeted there. It is now in the Tate collection in London.

The artist himself was cool about his most popular work. He is said to have called it a big knick-knack made to the usual formula. In the same 1898 exhibition he showed his rugged monument to the writer Balzac, which the public mocked and which he considered far more daring.
“The Kiss” moves people through bodies, not faces: an arm that pulls, a hand that hesitates, polished skin against raw rock.

So, back to the opening question. The faces are sealed away, the lips out of sight, the names forgotten by most people who stop here. And still nobody in that room, including the man by the window, has any doubt about what is happening.

quiz.question: Who are the two lovers?
quiz.explanation: They are the doomed couple Dante placed in Hell.

quiz.question: Why did Rodin remove the couple from “The Gates of Hell”?
options: They looked too happy among the damned
The group was too heavy for the doors
quiz.explanation: Their happiness clashed with the suffering shown on the doorway.

quiz.question: Who physically carved most of this marble?
quiz.explanation: Rodin modeled in clay and assistants translated the model into stone.

quiz.question: What does the rough rock under the figures do?
options: It hides a crack in the block
It makes the polished bodies look softer by contrast
It shows the sculpture was abandoned
quiz.explanation: Raw stone beside polished marble makes the skin seem warm and soft.

quiz.question: Which gesture shows that the woman takes the lead?
options: Her arm hooked around his neck, pulling him down
Her face turned to the viewer
quiz.explanation: She draws his head toward her and swings her leg over his.

facts.text: Rodin considered “The Kiss” his boldest work.
facts.explanation: He reportedly called it a big knick-knack and thought his Balzac far more daring.

facts.text: A marble version in England was once hidden under a sheet.
facts.explanation: At Lewes Town Hall it was railed off and covered for fear of exciting soldiers.

facts.text: The group was first designed as a wedding monument.
facts.explanation: It began as a pair of damned lovers for “The Gates of Hell”.
